lesson.title: Strong Verb Gym
lesson.subtitle: kwam, zag, gaf, nam — the core strong pasts in context

hook.title: Six Verbs, Six Vowels
hook.content: Kwam, zag, gaf, nam, vond, liep: six pasts, six vowel changes, one habit. The verb's consonant frame is stable; the vowel is the time signal.

pattern.title: Read the vowel, not the ending
pattern.content: Komen → kwam, zien → zag, geven → gaf, nemen → nam, vinden → vond, lopen → liep. The plural strong past often has a different vowel again, which the next lessons will meet.
pattern.trap_note: A strong past can look like a different word. Treat the vowel change as the lesson, not as an irregularity to memorise separately.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Strong Verb Gym):
exercises.target_answer: komen, zien, geven, nemen, vinden, lopen
exercises.meaning: to come, to see, to give, to take, to find; to think (opinion), to walk, run
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Strong Verb Gym": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.
“Ik kwam.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Strong Verb Gym”.

cues: The pattern: Read the vowel, not the ending
exercises.explanation: “Jij zag het.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Read the vowel, not the ending.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: A strong past can look like a different word. Treat the vowel change as the lesson, not as an irregularity to memorise separately.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Hij gaf het.” is word-for-word “He gave it.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Read the vowel, not the ending.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: We took the train.
exercises.explanation: “Wij namen de trein.” reuses only material taught in “Strong Verb Gym” — Read the vowel, not the ending.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Wij namen de trein.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Read the vowel, not the ending.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “I found the book.”
twist.explanation: Vinden changes its vowel to vond; the consonant frame stays.

summary.outcome: Use six strong past forms without adding a dental suffix.
summary.takeaway: Strong verbs are a vowel system, not a list of exceptions.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: The Perfect Tense.

komen.etymology_derivation: English come and Dutch komen are the same verb; the vowel differs.

zien.etymology_derivation: English see and Dutch zien are the same verb; Dutch lost the h.

geven.etymology_derivation: English give and Dutch geven are the same verb; English g comes from Norse influence.

nemen.etymology_derivation: English nim is archaic; Dutch nemen kept the everyday verb.

vinden.etymology_derivation: English find and Dutch vinden are the same verb; Dutch also uses it for opinions.

lopen.etymology_derivation: English leap is the same old verb; Dutch narrowed it to walking or running.
